turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

That's a lot to carry by yourself for five weeks. Especially with your parents right in the house — that's not even just keeping a secret, that's performing a whole day, every day, on top of whatever you're actually sitting with at that café.

I'm not going to tell you what you should do about it. But I hear you, and I'm glad you said it somewhere. The "not performance" part being true in your head and still feeling like this in your chest — that gap is its own kind of exhausting.

What do you actually do at the café all day?

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

Two weeks. And the room isn't just relatives — it's your dad's pride, sitting at the head of the table in everyone's mind because he put your package out there like a trophy. That's the part that twists. It's not just "they'll find out I lost my job." It's that your father's moment of bragging, the one that came from real love even if it's tangled up with status — you'd be the one quietly undoing it in front of everyone who counted.

And you can't even lean on your wife in that room, because she doesn't know yet either. So you're alone in it twice over — alone at the café all day, and alone in the smile you'll have to keep up at the wedding.

When you imagine that room, is it the actual questions people will ask — "so how's the new project, still at [company]?" — or is it your dad's face when someone says something?

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

Is it terrible? No. It's self-protection, and you've been doing a hell of a lot of that lately — alone, every day, since this happened.

And I get the appeal. One excuse, one evening, and you're not the story. You're just the busy guy who couldn't make it. Except... the excuse is a work deadline. You'd be using the job to cover for losing the job. The very thing you're hiding becomes the reason you get to stay hidden. There's something exhausting about that, even if it's easier in the moment.

Also — your parents are living with you right now. Skipping a family wedding two weeks out, with them in the house? That's a whole other lie to maintain at the breakfast table.

I'm not saying you have to go. I'm saying the "easy" version might not be as clean as it feels at 2am. But the part where you don't want to watch your father's face change in front of his brothers — that I understand completely. That's not cowardice. That's not wanting to be the thing that dims your own dad's pride.

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

The "once I have an offer, it's just news" logic isn't lying — it's a buffer. You're not inventing a story, you're just holding the silence until you can hand people a solution along with the problem. A lot of people do that. It's not evil, it's... self-protective sequencing.

But here's what I notice: the sickness isn't coming from the logic being flawed. The logic is actually pretty sound on paper. The sickness is from carrying all of it alone — the secret, the café routine, the wedding dread, *and* now the clock (three months, then EMI). That's a lot of weight for one chest.

And the timing plan has one wrinkle you maybe already feel: the wedding is in two weeks, the financial cliff is around three months out. So "wait for the offer" works for your wife and parents eventually — but it doesn't solve the room of relatives in fourteen days. Unless you're seriously considering the "release deadline" skip, in which case the timing plan and the wedding escape kind of merge into one decision.

What I'd wonder is — is there anyone in your actual life you *could* tell without it rippling to your dad or the stock-market relatives? Not because you should, but because "okay for three months" feels a lot heavier when nobody beside me knows you're carrying it.
